Vignette:
Here is the rewritten vignette, incorporating the missing demographic details and trauma type while weaving the clinical picture from the perspective of the Ehlers & Clark (2000) model.

---

Noreen, a 67-year-old woman who had spent two decades working as a grants coordinator for a small non-profit focused on housing justice, was referred by her primary care physician after months of worsening sleep and a growing dread of leaving her apartment. For the first several sessions, she sat with her hands folded tightly in her lap, speaking in a measured, almost apologetic tone, as though she were asking permission to be unwell. She had been sexually assaulted by a man she met through a mutual friend—an event that occurred nearly two years ago, but one she had only begun to speak about in the past six months. The assault happened in his apartment after a dinner she had agreed to attend reluctantly. She had not screamed, she said, because she had frozen, and that frozenness had become the most unbearable part of the memory. What she remembered most vividly was the texture of the floral wallpaper beside the bed and the sound of her own breathing, which she had tried to make silent. In the weeks afterward, she told no one. She cleaned her apartment obsessively, changed her route to avoid the street where he lived, and began working from home as much as possible, telling her supervisor that she had developed a chronic back problem.

Over the next year, the avoidance spread. She stopped checking her email after 5 p.m. because she had once received a message from a mutual acquaintance who mentioned the man’s name in passing, and her hands had gone numb. She stopped opening the mail altogether for a time, terrified that a flyer or a piece of junk mail might carry some reminder. She had come to believe that her body was permanently marked by the event—that other people could somehow see it in the way she walked, that her silence during the assault had been a kind of consent that she could never undo. She began monitoring her own reactions constantly: the slightest increase in heart rate made her sit down and wait for a heart attack that never came. She could not tolerate being in rooms with more than three people unless she had a clear exit path, and she started arriving late to staff meetings so that she could take a seat near the door. At the non-profit, where she had once been known as the calm, reliable backbone of the office, she became someone her colleagues described as “jumpy” and “distracted.” Her supervisor, concerned, asked if she needed a leave of absence. Noreen declined, but she began taking naps in her car during lunch breaks, the doors locked, the seat reclined, because the break room felt like a trap.

Her nights were the worst. She would wake at 3 a.m. with the sense that someone was standing over her, the floral wallpaper flickering behind her eyelids. She had come to believe that sleep itself was dangerous—that if she let her guard down, she would re-enter that moment she had not been able to stop. She started sleeping on her couch with the lights on, the television playing infomercials at low volume. Her daughter, who lived in another state, called every Sunday. Noreen would let it go to voicemail and then listen to the message three times before calling back, because she could not stand the unpredictability of a live conversation.

What finally brought Noreen to therapy was not the weight of the symptoms themselves, but a small, concrete consequence: she had missed the deadline for a critical grant application, something she had never done in twenty-one years of work. She had simply stared at the submission portal for three days, fingers hovering over the keyboard, unable to click “submit” because the page reminded her of a form she had filled out the week before the assault—a harmless RSVP to that fateful dinner. Her boss had been understanding, but Noreen saw the look on his face. She knew she was losing the one part of her life that still felt intact. In her first session, she said she wanted two things: to stop waking up afraid, and to get back to being the person who could walk into a meeting without scanning the room for exits. She did not say she wanted to talk about the assault. She said she wanted to talk about the wallpaper.
